transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?

Well... ever since my heart stopped about two and a half years ago, I go out of my way not to think or talk about what happened or anything to do with doctors. My wife finally convinced me to mention it to my cardiologist, which is how I ended up being referred to you.
Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'going out of your way not to think or talk about what happened' - does this avoidance cause you significant distress or interfere with your daily life?

Whenever my family brings up my heart or doctor visits, I'll change the subject or leave the room just to avoid thinking about it. It has really shrunk my life—I've stopped organizing events at the senior center and going on walks with friends, so now I mostly stay home and let my wife handle all my appointments because it's just too much.
Do you ever experience unwanted memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about the event when your heart stopped, even when you're not trying to think about it?

Yes, they come out of nowhere when I'm just watching TV or sitting in the garden. I'll suddenly see myself lying on the kitchen floor again and hear my wife screaming my name. My chest tightens up just like it did that day, and it feels like I'm about to die all over again.

Do you find yourself constantly on the lookout for potential dangers or threats to your health, even when there's no obvious reason to be concerned, such as always checking your pulse or blood pressure?

Yes, I am constantly on edge and find myself checking my pulse all the time. When I do go out, I'm always looking for the nearest phone and exit, and at night I lie awake listening for any strange noises. I just feel like I have to be ready because my body or the world could turn on me again at any second.

Can you describe any specific physical symptoms or complaints you've been experiencing that you haven't mentioned yet, such as pain, gastrointestinal issues, or other bodily concerns that seem unrelated to your heart condition?

No, I haven't really experienced other physical complaints like pain or stomach issues. My main concerns are really just the ones we've already talked about, with my heart anxiety and trying to avoid those memories.

Can you estimate how much time you spend each day thinking about or trying to avoid thoughts of the event when your heart stopped, and has this changed over the two and a half years since it happened?

It honestly feels like a constant, daily struggle that is always in the back of my mind, with those thoughts popping up out of nowhere throughout the day. I have to put a lot of active effort into avoiding them, and this pattern hasn't let up at all over the last two and a half years.
Do you ever feel detached from yourself or the world around you, as if you're observing things from outside your body or as if things aren't real?
No, I don't really experience those kinds of feelings. I've never felt detached from my own body or felt like the things around me aren't real.

Do you experience any feelings of guilt or shame related to the event when your heart stopped, such as feeling like you're a burden to your family or that you somehow could have prevented what happened?

Yes, I do feel a lot of guilt about it. Even though the doctors told me it was just an electrical issue with my heart, I can't shake the feeling that I brought it on myself. I keep thinking that if I had taken better care of my health and not brushed off little warning signs over the years, it might not have happened.
Have you noticed any difficulty falling or staying asleep, or do you have problems with concentration due to being constantly on edge and vigilant for potential threats?

Yes, my sleep is terrible because I lie awake for hours and jerk awake at the slightest sound, so I never feel truly rested. I'm not sure if my concentration is affected, but being constantly on edge and listening for noises at night definitely keeps me from getting any real peace.

Have you tried to confront or face your fears about your heart condition directly, or do you think you would benefit from trying to gradually become comfortable with the things you're currently avoiding?

No, I haven't tried to face them at all; instead, I do everything I can to run away, like changing the subject, leaving the room, or avoiding walks near the hospital. While the idea of gradually facing those fears might make sense in theory, the actual thought of doing it right now feels completely overwhelming and terrifying.

You mentioned earlier that you don't feel detached from yourself or the world, but can you tell me more about what you mean by that and if you've ever had any moments where you felt like you were in a dream or things seemed unreal, even if it was just for a brief instant?

No, I can't say I've ever felt like I was in a dream or that things around me weren't real, even for a second. I always feel very present in my body and my surroundings, even though I'm constantly anxious and on edge.
Can you elaborate on how your feelings of guilt about the heart event have affected your self-perception or relationships with others, such as feeling like a burden or having a negative self-image?

I constantly blame myself for the collapse, feeling like my body is a failing, ticking time bomb because I neglected my health for years. This has made me feel like a massive burden to my wife, who now has to manage all my appointments and plans. I also feel terrible because I've been snapping at her over silly things, like the TV volume or when she reminds me to take my pills.
Have you considered seeking forgiveness from yourself for what happened, or do you think that's something you're not ready to confront yet?

It's very hard to forgive myself because I still carry this strong feeling that I brought the collapse on myself by ignoring my health over the years. Honestly, confronting that guilt is incredibly difficult, and I've mostly just been avoiding it because it feels too overwhelming to face.

You've mentioned a lot of anxiety and avoidance related to your heart condition, but can you tell me if you've experienced any other unexplained physical symptoms, like numbness, tingling, or pain in different parts of your body, that don't seem directly related to your heart?

No, I haven't really experienced those kinds of physical symptoms like numbness, tingling, or unexplained pain. The physical feelings I do get are mostly just my chest tightening or my heart racing when I get anxious or reminded of what happened.
